# Product Notes: The Drum-40 Roaster

Internal spec notes for the Drum-40, our main production roaster since 2022.
Written up after the second maintenance cycle so we'd stop losing this
knowledge every time someone leaves.

## Capacity and throughput

Rated for 40lb green coffee per batch, though we run it closer to 35lb in
practice — pushing full capacity tends to uneven the roast toward the back of
the drum. A full day is six to seven batches depending on bean density; denser
naturals take longer to come up to first crack and that adds maybe four minutes
per batch over washed coffees.

## Known quirks

The gas valve sticks slightly below 20% output, so ramping down slowly at the
end of a roast can undershoot for a few seconds before catching up. This isn't
a defect, it's just how this un

end of a roast can undershoot for a few seconds before catching up. This isn't
a defect, it's just how this unit behaves — don't chase it by overcorrecting,
you'll get a wavier temperature curve than if you just let it settle.

Batch three of any given day tends to run about 8°F hotter at first crack than
batch one, because the drum itself is still carrying heat. Roasters who don't
account for this end up with an inconsistent third batch — this is the single
most common mistake we see from people in their first month.

Chaff needs clearing every single batch, not just at the end of the day — it's

Anything involving the gas line or the drum motor: call it in, don't attempt a

# Git Version Control System

Git is a distributed version control system that tracks changes in any set of computer files, usually used for coordinating work among programmers collaboratively developing source code during software development. Its goals include speed, data integrity, and support for distributed, non-linear workflows (thousands of parallel branches running on different systems). 

Git was created by Linus Torvalds in 2005 for the development of the Linux kernel, with other kernel developers contributing to its initial development. Since 2005, Junio Hamano has been the core maintainer. 

## Features

Git's design was inspired by BitKeeper and Monotone. Git was originally designed as a low-level version control system engine over which others could write front ends, such as

by BitKeeper and Monotone. Git was originally designed as a low-level version control system engine over which others could write front ends, such as Cogito or StGit. However, the core Git project has since become a complete version control system usable directly.

**Data Storage**
Unlike most older version control systems (such as SVN and CVS) which store file differences (deltas), Git stores data as a series of snapshots. Every time you commit, or save the state of your project, Git basically takes a picture of what all your files look like at that moment and stores a reference to that snapshot. To be efficient, if files have not changed, Git doesn't store the file again, just a link to the previous identical file it has already stored.

**Local Operations**
Most operations in Git require only local files and resources to operate — generally no information is needed from another computer on your network. Because you have the entire history of the project right there on your local disk, most operations seem almost instantaneous. 

**States**
Git has three main states that your files can reside in:
1. **Committed**: Data is safely stored in your local database.
2. **Modified**: You have changed the file but have not committed it to your database yet.
3. **Staged**: You have marked a modified file in its current version to go into your next commit snapshot.

# Getting Set Up at Fernhollow Coffee Roasters

Welcome aboard. This doc covers the basics for your first two weeks — read it once,
then keep it around for reference because half of this won't stick the first time.

## Your first day

Show up at the Elm Street roastery, not the retail counter on 5th. Ring the side
door if it's before 8am; the front doesn't unlock until Maria gets in. You'll be
paired with a roasting lead for the first three shifts — don't touch the drum
roaster alone until week three, no exceptions, even if you've run one before at
a previous job. Every machine here has its own quirks and we've had two burnt
batches this year from people who "already knew how."

## Pay and scheduling

Payroll runs biweekly, direct deposit hits Thursdays. Timesheets are due Monday
by noon for the prior two weeks — late submissions get paid the following cycle,
not retroactively, so don't sit on it. Scheduling is done through the shared
calendar; shift swaps need sign-off from whoever's running that day, not just a
text to the person you're swapping with.

## Tasting and quality control

Every roaster does a cupping session at 7:30am before the first roast of the day.
This isn't optional and it isn't just for the head roasters — everyone's palate
matters here, including yours on day one. We're looking for consistency batch to
batch more than we're looking for "good" coffee; a roast that's slightly off but
predictable is more use

y one. We're looking for consistency batch to
batch more than we're looking for "good" coffee; a roast that's slightly off but
predictable is more useful to us than a great roast we can't repeat.

## Time off

Two weeks paid to start, accruing from day one but not usable until after your
90-day mark. After that it's your call when you take it, just give at least two
weeks notice for anything longer than three days so we can cover the floor.
Sick days are separate and don't need advance notice, obviously.

## Who to ask

- Roasting questions: whoever's lead that shift, then Dev if they're stuck
- Payroll or HR stuff: Priya, she's usually in Tuesday–Friday
- Anything about the retail side: that's a different building and a different
  manual, ask Sam over there
